lessons.title: The Minimum Variance Portfolio: The Safest Point on the Frontier

children.text: Lesson 2 found the minimum-variance point on the Nifty IT and Nifty Bank curve by scanning eleven weight combinations and reading off the smallest risk number, landing on an approximate 30% Nifty IT. Scanning works, but it is an approximation, and it does not scale past a handful of assets. This lesson derives the exact formula, so the safest point on any two-asset frontier is one calculation away, not a search.

body.text: The minimum-variance portfolio is not found by guessing weights and checking the risk. It falls straight out of calculus: set the rate of change of portfolio variance, with respect to weight, to zero, and solve.

children.text: Minimizing Variance: One Derivative, One Formula
Start from Lesson 2 of Chapter 2's formula, with w2 replaced by 1 minus w1 so variance is written purely as a function of w1.

body.caption: Portfolio variance as a function of a single variable, w1.
Set the derivative to zero: this is the flattest point on the curve, where variance stops falling and starts rising.
Solving for w1 gives the exact minimum-variance weight. w2* is simply 1 minus w1*.

children.text: Applying It: the Exact Nifty IT / Nifty Bank Minimum
Using Chapter 2's numbers, Var(IT) = 39.81, Var(Bank) = 28.69, Cov(IT, Bank) = 21.38:

body.label: Exact minimum-variance weight
body.context: (28.69 - 21.38) / (39.81 + 28.69 - 2 x 21.38) = 7.31 / 25.74 = 0.284. This lands slightly below the table's rounded 30% reading, and gives an annualized volatility of 17.87%, exact rather than approximate.

children.text: A Clean Special Case: Equal-Variance Assets

If two assets happen to share the same variance, set sigma1 squared equal to sigma2 squared equal to sigma squared in the formula. The Cov12 terms do not cancel, but the sigma squared terms do, in a specific way:

body.caption: Equal individual risk always means a 50/50 minimum-variance split, whatever the correlation happens to be, as long as it is not exactly 1.

body.text: This is a genuinely useful shortcut: whenever two assets are similarly volatile, you already know the minimum-variance split is close to even, without calculating anything. The correlation number still decides HOW LOW that minimum risk gets, but it stops mattering for WHERE the minimum sits, once variances are equal.

children.text: TCS and Maruti Suzuki's variances were NOT equal: 2.9167 for TCS against 3.9167 for Maruti Suzuki. The 50/50 split back in Chapter 1 was chosen for the case study, not because it was proven optimal. Running the actual formula settles the question.

body.caption: TCS and Maruti Suzuki: fixed 50/50 versus the true minimum-variance weight

body.text: 1.482% is only marginally below 1.500%, a small improvement, not a dramatic one. That is itself a useful lesson: 50/50 was never far from optimal for this particular pair, but "close to optimal" and "optimal" are not the same claim, and only the formula can tell you which one you actually have. Chapter 1 got lucky with a round number. This formula removes the luck.

children.text: Extending to N Assets: the Matrix Formula

The same calculus, done with the covariance matrix from Chapter 2, produces a matrix version of the same idea. Full derivation and the general optimization machinery are Lesson 4's job. For now, here is the formula, and what it does when pointed at real data.

body.caption: The unconstrained N-asset minimum-variance weights. Sigma inverse is the inverted covariance matrix, and 1 is a column of ones. The denominator simply rescales the result so the weights sum to 1.

body.code:
import numpy as np

# TCS, Maruti Suzuki, HDFC Bank, HUL covariance matrix from Chapter 2, Lesson 3
cov_matrix = np.array([
    [484.0, 184.8, 137.5, 39.6],
    [184.8, 784.0, 245.0, 75.6],
    [137.5, 245.0, 625.0, 90.0],
    [39.6,  75.6,  90.0,  324.0],
])

ones = np.ones(4)
inv_cov = np.linalg.inv(cov_matrix)
weights = (inv_cov @ ones) / (ones @ inv_cov @ ones)
min_variance = 1 / (ones @ inv_cov @ ones)

names = ["TCS", "Maruti Suzuki", "HDFC Bank", "HUL"]
for n, w in zip(names, weights):
    print(f"{n}: {w*100:.2f}%")
print(f"Minimum annualized volatility: {np.sqrt(min_variance):.2f}%")
body.caption: Same covariance matrix Lesson 3 of Chapter 2 built by hand, now solved directly for its minimum-variance weights.

body.text: This four-stock minimum-variance portfolio reaches 13.80% annualized volatility, below the 15.33% found for the equal-weighted version of the same four stocks back in Chapter 2, and far below the naive 23.25% average of their individual volatilities. Notice HUL, the least volatile and least correlated stock in the group, receives the largest weight by far, at 49.52%. The formula is not choosing "good stocks." It is choosing whichever combination cancels out the most risk, which tends to favor calmer, more independent assets.

This formula has no constraint against negative weights. It happened to return all-positive weights here, but with a different set of assets, it can easily call for a short position, which may be impractical, costly, or simply not permitted in a given account. It also ignores expected return completely, it only minimizes risk. Lesson 4 builds the full efficient frontier, which brings expected return back into the picture, and Chapter 6 covers adding real-world constraints like a no-short-selling rule.

body.title: Solve for a new minimum-variance weight
body.prompt: Two assets have Var1 = 10, Var2 = 15, and Cov12 = 4 (all in percent-squared). What is the minimum-variance weight in Asset 1?

body.title: The equal-variance shortcut
body.question: Two assets have equal variance, but a correlation of 0.4 rather than 0. What is their minimum-variance weight split?
options: It cannot be determined without knowing the exact variance values
50% / 50%, since equal variance always produces an even split at the minimum-variance point, regardless of correlation
It depends entirely on the correlation: 0.4 correlation means roughly 40% / 60%
100% in whichever asset has the lower correlation with the other
body.explanation: As this lesson's algebra showed, when sigma1 equals sigma2, the formula collapses to exactly 1/2, regardless of the specific correlation value, as long as it is not exactly 1. Correlation changes how low the resulting minimum risk is, but not where the minimum-variance weight sits.

cards.definition: w1* = (Var2 - Cov12) / (Var1 + Var2 - 2 Cov12), found by setting the derivative of portfolio variance with respect to w1 to zero.
When two assets have equal variance, their minimum-variance split is always 50/50, regardless of their correlation (provided it is not exactly 1).
w* = (Sigma inverse x 1) / (1 transpose x Sigma inverse x 1), the matrix generalization of the two-asset formula, ignoring expected return and any weight constraints.

points: The minimum-variance weight for two assets has a closed-form formula, derived by setting the derivative of portfolio variance to zero: no scanning or guessing required.
Applied exactly to Nifty IT and Nifty Bank, the true minimum sits at 28.4% Nifty IT, close to but more precise than the 30% found earlier by scanning a table.
When two assets share the same variance, their minimum-variance split is always exactly 50/50, whatever their correlation, as long as it is below 1.
Revisiting Chapter 1's TCS and Maruti Suzuki case study with the actual formula shows 50/50 was close to, but not exactly, optimal: the true minimum sits at 60.7% TCS, only marginally lower in risk.
The same idea extends to N assets through a matrix formula, w* = Sigma inverse x 1, normalized to sum to 1, which can return negative (short) weights and ignores expected return entirely.
This is only half of what a real efficient frontier needs. Lesson 4 brings expected return back into the optimization, solving for the full frontier rather than only its single lowest-risk point.
